title: I Have Called You by Name
paragraphs:
I Have Called You by Name
The Four Words That Can Rescue a Soul From Losing Itself
There are wounds so deep that no one sees them.
They hide behind successful careers, smiling family photos, Sunday church attendance, and carefully crafted social media posts.
Some wounds never bleed outward.
They bleed identity.
The quiet fear that maybe you are forgotten.
Maybe unseen.
Maybe replaceable.
Maybe God knows humanity generally but not you personally.
Maybe heaven knows your category but not your name.
And if there is one fear that haunts the human heart from childhood to old age, it is this:
"Do I truly matter?"
The world teaches us to build an identity.
God reveals that identity is something He gives.
That distinction changes everything.

Buried within one of Scripture's most breathtaking declarations is a sentence that has carried broken believers through persecution, grief, betrayal, addiction, failure, loneliness, and seasons where God felt painfully silent.
The Lord says:
"Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name; you are Mine." (Isaiah 43:1)
Most people read those words quickly.
But they are among the most intimate words God ever speaks to His people.
To understand their depth, we must enter the ancient world behind the text.
The original Hebrew reads:

וָאֶקְרָא בְשִׁמְךָ לִי־אָתָּה
Va'eqra b'shimkha, li attah.
A faithful translation is:
"I have called you by your name; you belong to Me."
Notice what God does not say.
He does not say:
"I have called your group."
"I have called your nation."
"I have called your denomination."
"I have called your generation."
He says:
"I have called you by your name."
The Hebrew word שֵׁם (shem) means more than a label.
In biblical thought, a name represented identity, character, destiny, reputation, purpose, and calling.
To know someone's name was to know something about their essence.
When God says He has called someone by name, He is not merely proving recognition.
He is declaring ownership, relationship, and intentionality.
This is deeply significant because Isaiah was written to people facing national devastation.
Israel would experience judgment, exile, loss, humiliation, and uncertainty.
Everything familiar would collapse.
Yet God tells them that even when circumstances scream abandonment, they remain known.
Not generally.
Personally.
The same God who names stars also names people.
The same God who governs galaxies knows individual hearts.
The same God who rules eternity speaks personally into human history.
This theme echoes throughout the entire Bible.
When Hagar fled into the wilderness, abandoned and pregnant, she discovered something astonishing.
She encountered the God who sees.
She called Him:
אֵל רֳאִי (El Roi)
"The God Who Sees Me."
Not the God who sees crowds.
The God who sees me.
When Samuel was searching for Israel's future king, God rejected every outward qualification before choosing David.
When Elijah believed he was alone, God knew exactly where he was hiding.
When Zacchaeus climbed a tree just to glimpse Jesus, Christ stopped beneath the branches and called him by name.
When Lazarus lay dead in a tomb, Jesus called him by name.
When Mary Magdalene stood weeping outside an empty grave, believing all hope was lost, Jesus spoke a single word:
"Mary."
Everything changed.
One word.
One name.
One moment.
The Gospel is filled with names.
Because salvation is personal.
Jesus did not come merely to save humanity as a concept.
He came to save people.
Individuals.
Real names.
Real stories.
Real failures.
Real redemption.
This is why one of the most beautiful images in Scripture appears in John 10.
Jesus says:
"The good shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out."
The Greek text reads:

κατ' ὄνομα
kat' onoma
"By name."
Not by number.
Not by category.
Not by usefulness.
Not by performance.
By name.
In the ancient Near East, shepherds often knew their sheep individually.
The image Jesus chooses is intentional.
The Good Shepherd knows every scar, every weakness, every tendency to wander, every fear, every hidden wound.
Nothing surprises Him.
Nothing escapes Him.
This truth becomes even more astonishing when we realize what God knows about us.
He knows every sin.
Every compromise.
Every secret.
Every rebellion.
Every shameful memory.
And still He calls.
That is the scandal of grace.
Humanity expects rejection after exposure.
The Gospel reveals acceptance through redemption.
This does not mean God ignores sin.
Far from it.
The cross proves how seriously God takes sin.
But the cross also proves how seriously God takes sinners.
At Calvary, justice and mercy kissed.
There, Jesus carried every accusation that could ever separate us from God.
Isaiah's promise becomes fully realized in Christ.
"I have redeemed you."
The Hebrew word for redeemed is גָּאַל (ga'al).
It refers to a kinsman-redeemer.
Someone who steps in personally to rescue, restore, and reclaim what was lost.
Jesus becomes our ultimate Redeemer.
Not a distant rescuer.
A family Redeemer.
A covenant Redeemer.
A sacrificial Redeemer.
This means your identity is no longer determined by your worst chapter.
Your addiction is not your name.
Your divorce is not your name.
Your failure is not your name.
Your anxiety is not your name.
Your depression is not your name.
Your past is not your name.
Your shame is not your name.
The world names people according to wounds.
Jesus names people according to redemption.
Simon becomes Peter.
Saul becomes Paul.
Failures become disciples.
Sinners become saints.
Orphans become sons and daughters.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You may feel forgotten.
You may feel invisible.
You may feel like everyone else has purpose while you are wandering through confusion.
You may feel that your mistakes have permanently defined you.
But Scripture tells another story.
The God who formed you knows your name.
The God who redeemed you knows your story.
The God who calls you knows your future.
Nothing about you is accidental.
Nothing about your life has escaped His attention.
Nothing about your pain is wasted.
Nothing about your scars is beyond His ability to transform.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
From brokenness to restoration.
From rebellion to redemption.
From death to life.
And one day, the Bible says believers will receive a new name.
Revelation 2:17 speaks of a white stone with a name known fully by God.
The journey that began with God calling us by name culminates in eternity where our identity is fully restored in Christ.
Imagine that.
The God who knew your name before you were born.
The God who knew your failures before you committed them.
The God who loved you before you loved Him.
The God who redeemed you through the blood of Jesus.
The God who never lost sight of you for a single second.
That God still calls.
Not because you earned it.
Not because you deserve it.
Because grace has always been His plan.
Perhaps today is the day you stop listening to the names the world has given you.
Perhaps today is the day you believe the name spoken over you by the One who made you.
The One who says:
"Fear not."
"I have redeemed you."
"I have called you by name."
"You are Mine."
Sit with those words for a moment.
Read them slowly.
Let them settle into places that have been wounded for years.
Because if God calls you by name, you are not forgotten.
If God calls you by name, you are not abandoned.
If God calls you by name, you are not beyond redemption.
If God calls you by name, your story is not over.
Most importantly, support the mission of proclaiming Jesus Christ to a world desperately searching for identity.
Before you leave, be honest:
When was the last time you truly believed God was speaking to you personally?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else needs today.
The God who knows your name has never once forgotten your story.
